common_name: Rubin Hens and Chicks (Deep Ruby-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Rubin is a long-established sempervivum cultivar valued for rosettes that turn a saturated ruby to near-blackish red across almost the entire leaf, with color deepening rather than washing out under strong summer sun and cold autumn nights. Press offsets directly onto the surface of sharply drained, mineral-heavy soil, since any organic richness or lingering moisture around the crown invites rot. It forms a slowly spreading mat as offsets fill in around each parent rosette, making it useful for color contrast against the greens and blues of companion sempervivum cultivars in troughs and crevice gardens. Give it a full day of sun to hold its darkest tone; in shade the color fades toward dull green and rosettes stretch and loosen.

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Native to rocky outcrops and old walls across the Balkans and central Europe, marbled houseleek forms mid-sized green rosettes whose leaf tips flush deep wine-red, with the two tones blending into a mottled, marbled pattern that is most pronounced in lean soil and strong sun. Press offsets onto the surface of sharply drained gravelly or rocky soil, since standing moisture around the crown causes rapid rot regardless of how cold-hardy the species is. It spreads at a moderate pace by short-stemmed offsets, filling crevices and trough plantings within a couple of seasons. Mature rosettes send up a stout stalk of star-shaped pink-purple flowers once, then die back as the surrounding offsets continue the clump.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or set container stock in fast-draining, lean succulent mix in full sun to light afternoon shade; bring indoors well before first frost, since Aeonium urbicum has no cold tolerance.

directions: Aeonium urbicum, a Canary Islands native, grows on a mostly unbranched upright stem topped with a large, flat, saucer-shaped rosette of green leaves often edged in a fine reddish line, quite distinct from the low, branching habit of Aeonium arboreum types. Grow it in fast-draining, lean soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, watering only when the soil has dried and withholding water almost entirely during its summer dormancy. Like other aeoniums it grows actively through the cool months and rests in high summer heat, so ease off feeding and watering as temperatures climb. A given rosette flowers only once, on a tall pyramidal spike of starry white-pink blooms, and then that growing point dies, though offsets at the base of the stem usually keep the plant going.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Noble Aeonium (Giant Solitary Bronze Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Set container-grown offsets or rooted rosettes in fast-draining, lean succulent mix in full sun to light afternoon shade; protect from any frost.

directions: Native to La Palma in the Canary Islands, Aeonium nobile forms a single enormous rosette, sometimes over a foot across, of thick, waxy, bronze-red to olive-green leaves held nearly stemless just above the soil, making it one of the most dramatic solitary succulents in the genus. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, watering only as the mix dries and cutting back almost entirely during summer dormancy. The rosette is monocarpic, sending up a tall spike of star-shaped reddish flowers once it reaches maturity and then dying back, though it usually produces one or more basal offsets beforehand that can be separated and grown on. Keep it dry and cool over winter, since excess moisture combined with cold is the most common cause of rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in a fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade; avoid direct hot midday sun, which scorches the leaves.

directions: This dwarf South African species forms small clumps of thick, dark green, white-spotted leaves arranged in two flat ranks on young rosettes before spiraling slightly with age, staying compact enough for a small pot or a crowded dish garden. Grow in a fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light or light shade, since Gasteria liliputana naturally grows tucked under rocks and shrubs in habitat and scorches in strong direct sun. Water only when the soil has dried out fully and withhold water almost entirely in winter. It offsets readily from the base, forming a tight, low clump that is easily divided for propagation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in a fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade, protecting from direct hot midday sun.

directions: Gasteria batesiana forms a low, compact rosette of thick, dark green to almost blackish leaves covered in raised, wart-like tubercles, giving it a rugged, textured look that sets it apart from the smoother-leaved gasterias. Native to the Great Fish River valley of South Africa's Eastern Cape, it naturally grows in the dappled shade of shrubs and rock overhangs, so bright indirect light or light shade suits it far better than harsh direct sun, which can scorch the leaves. Plant in a fast-draining succulent mix and water only once the soil has dried out completely, cutting back further in winter. It slowly forms small offsetting clumps that can be divided once they crowd their pot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun; allow cut ends to callus for several days before inserting into soil.

directions: Native to the winter-rainfall Western Cape of South Africa, Cotyledon papillaris is a low, sprawling, mat-forming species with small, gray-green, egg-shaped leaves densely covered in fine papillae that give the foliage a soft, slightly velvety texture. Grow in full sun in extremely well-drained, gritty soil, and let the soil dry completely between waterings, since it is markedly more rot-prone than the larger, more familiar Cotyledon orbiculata. Its trailing stems root readily where they touch the ground, so it spreads gradually into a loose groundcover in rock gardens or spills attractively over the edge of a container. Clusters of small orange to red bell-shaped flowers appear on short stalks above the foliage in summer.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root leaf or offset cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright light with some protection from the most intense midday sun; avoid overhead watering, which strips the powdery farina.

directions: Discovered in Oaxaca, Mexico, Echeveria laui is prized among collectors for its thick, rounded, powder-blue-white leaves coated in an unusually heavy layer of farina, giving the compact rosette an almost frosted, chalky appearance unmatched by most other species in the genus. Because that farina rubs off permanently at a touch and washes away with overhead watering, it is best grown under cover or with a rain-sheltered overhang and watered carefully at the soil line rather than from above. Give it bright light with some shielding from the harshest midday sun, which can still scorch the leaf tips despite the plant's dry native habitat. It offsets slowly, so patient propagation from individual leaves or small basal offsets is the usual way to increase a collection.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Giant Echeveria (Large Bronze Undulate-Leaf Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to light shade; older plants develop a short trunk and benefit from being staked or grown where the top-heavy rosette is supported.

directions: Native to central Mexico, Echeveria gibbiflora is one of the largest species in the genus, forming a substantial rosette of broad, spoon-shaped, gray-green to purplish-bronze leaves with distinctly undulate, crimped margins on a stem that thickens into a short trunk with age. Grow in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since intense uninterrupted sun in very hot climates can scorch the broad leaves. It tolerates brief cool snaps better than many smaller echeverias but still needs winter protection from any real frost. In fall it sends up tall, arching flower stalks lined with red-orange, bell-shaped blooms that are a magnet for hummingbirds, after which the rosette continues growing rather than dying back.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
